blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — OTC loperamide bloody-stool warning
stem: A client with acute diarrhea reports bloody stool and asks whether to take OTC loperamide. What should the nurse advise?

options.A: Do not take loperamide; bloody or black stool is specifically listed in the OTC label as a condition in which the drug should not be used.
options.B: Take the labeled adult dose and increase clear fluids because bloody stool does not change the usual self-treatment directions for acute diarrhea.
options.C: Take one-half of the labeled dose and stop if the diarrhea continues for more than 2 days because dose reduction addresses the bleeding concern.
options.D: Use loperamide after the next loose stool if there is no fever because absence of fever makes self-treatment appropriate despite bloody stool.

rationale: Current OTC loperamide labeling states under 'Do not use' that the product should not be used when stool is bloody or black. Therefore A is correct. The label separately advises clear fluids, sets dosing limits, and instructs users to stop and ask a doctor if diarrhea lasts more than 2 days, but none of those directions overrides the explicit bloody-stool restriction. Absence of fever also does not make self-treatment appropriate when bloody stool is present.
educational_objective: Recognize bloody or black stool as a labeled situation in which OTC loperamide should not be used.
source_organization: DailyMed (U.S. National Library of Medicine) / FDA OTC labeling
source_version_date: SPL version 1; effective June 3, 2026; published June 4, 2026; accessed 2026-08-26
source_locator: Drug Facts — Warnings: Do not use if you have bloody or black stool; Ask a doctor before use; Stop use and ask a doctor; Directions.
source_claim_supported: The OTC loperamide label states not to use the drug if stool is bloody or black; fever and mucus in stool require medical advice before use, and persistent diarrhea beyond 2 days requires stopping and asking a doctor.
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12/PDF p.16: educate client about medications; review pertinent data prior to medication administration; administer medications safely.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four choices as plausible self-treatment decisions without the original absolute-word distractor cue.
Length-balanced the options and anchored the key to the exact current OTC 'Do not use' warning.
audit_note: Independent adversarial review confirms A uniquely follows the current OTC label. B–D use plausible elements of diarrhea self-care but improperly override the explicit bloody-stool restriction; lengths are closely matched and no cue remains.
